questions.q: An AC induction motor has two main parts and transforms electrical energy mainly into what form of energy?
options: The two main parts are the stator and the rotor, and it transforms electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy
The two main parts are the brushes and the commutator, and it transforms chemical energy into electrical energy
The two main parts are the primary and secondary coils, and it transforms rotational kinetic energy into electrical energy
The two main parts are the slip rings and the armature, and it transforms electrical energy into chemical energy
questions.explanation: As with DC motors and generators, an AC motor has two main parts: the stator and the rotor. The stator is the stationary part that provides the external magnetic field which produces a torque on the rotor, and electrical energy is usually transformed into rotational kinetic energy. In Australia the AC supply frequency is 50 Hz.

questions.q: Why is an AC induction motor called an 'induction' motor?
options: Because no current passes through the rotor directly from the mains supply; the current in the rotor is induced in the conductors of the cage by a changing magnetic field
Because the rotor is a permanent magnet that was induced during manufacture
Because an induction coil must charge the rotor before the motor will run
Because brushes induce the supply current directly into the commutator of the rotor
questions.explanation: Induction motors are so named because a changing magnetic field set up in the stator induces a current in the rotor, similar to a transformer. No current passes through the rotor directly from the mains supply — the current in the rotor bars is induced by the changing magnetic field.

questions.q: In a squirrel-cage rotor, why are the conductor bars encased in a laminated iron core?
options: The iron intensifies the magnetic field passing through the rotor conductors, while the laminations decrease the heating losses due to eddy currents
The iron stores charge for the rotor, while the laminations increase the eddy currents that drive it
The iron insulates the bars, while the laminations carry the mains supply current into the rotor
The iron reduces the magnetic field, while the laminations short-circuit the two end rings together
questions.explanation: The bars and end rings of the squirrel-cage rotor are encased in a laminated iron armature. The iron intensifies the magnetic field passing through the conductors of the rotor cage, making the induced current and torque larger, and the laminations decrease the heating losses due to eddy currents in the core itself.

questions.q: Describe the construction of a squirrel-cage rotor.
keyPoints: It consists of a number of conducting bars made of either aluminium or copper.
The bars are attached to two end rings at either end; the end rings 'short-circuit' the bars and allow a current to flow from one side of the cage to the other.
The bars and end rings are encased in a laminated iron armature mounted on a shaft that passes out of the motor.
questions.explanation: If you recalled aluminium or copper bars, the two short-circuiting end rings, and the laminated iron core, grade yourself Good or Easy. The end rings providing a closed conducting path are essential — that is what lets the induced EMF drive a current.

questions.q: How does the rotating magnetic field of the stator produce a force on the bars of the squirrel cage?
options: The relative movement of the bars through the magnetic field creates a current in the bars, and bars carrying a current in a magnetic field experience a force, so the cage is forced to chase the magnetic field
The magnetic field charges the bars by direct contact, and like charges then repel the field away
The bars heat up and expand, mechanically pushing the rotor around inside the stator
Slip rings feed the supply current to the bars, which then magnetically attract the stator poles
questions.explanation: As the magnetic field rotates within the stator it passes over the bars of the cage — the same effect as the bars moving in the opposite direction through a stationary field. This relative movement of the bars through the magnetic field creates a current; the current-carrying bars then experience a force in the same direction as the movement of the field, so the cage is forced to chase the magnetic field around inside the stator.

questions.q: What would happen if the bars of the squirrel cage rotated at exactly the same rate as the rotating magnetic field?
options: There would be no relative movement between the bars and the magnetic field, so there would be no induced current and no force
The induced current would reach its maximum value, giving the greatest possible force on the rotor
The motor would produce the same force but would consume no electrical power at all
The two end rings would short-circuit and bring the rotor to an instant stop
questions.explanation: If the bars of the squirrel cage rotated at exactly the same rate as the magnetic field, there would be no relative movement between the bars and the field, and therefore no induced current and no force. For the cage to experience a force there must be relative movement — the cage must constantly 'slip' behind the magnetic field.

questions.q: What is slip, and explain why it is necessary for the operation of a squirrel-cage induction motor.
keyPoints: Slip (slip speed) is the difference in rotational speed between the cage (rotor) and the rotating magnetic field of the stator.
There must be relative movement between the bars and the field for a current to be induced and a force to be produced — so the rotor always runs slower than the field when doing work.
Under a heavier load the cage slows, the amount of slip increases, so the relative movement, the induced current and the magnetic force are all increased.
questions.explanation: Slip is not a defect: with no slip there is no relative movement, no induced current and no force. The self-regulating point (more load -> more slip -> more current -> more force) is the high-band idea.

questions.q: A flat loop of area 0.3 m² lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength B = 0.05 T. Calculate the magnetic flux through the loop.
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux is the perpendicular field strength multiplied by the area, \(\phi_B = B_\perp \times A\). With the field perpendicular to the loop, \(\phi_B = 0.05 \times 0.3 = 0.015\,\mathrm{Wb}\). This is the same sample-problem method the textbook uses to calculate magnetic flux.

questions.q: A three-phase induction motor has a synchronous (field) speed of 3000 rpm. Under load the rotor turns at 2880 rpm. Calculate the slip speed and the slip expressed as a fraction.
questions.given: synchronous speed = 3000 rpm,  rotor speed = 2880 rpm
working: slip speed = synchronous speed − rotor speed
questions.explanation: The slip speed is the gap between the field's synchronous speed and the rotor's actual speed: 3000 − 2880 = 120 rpm, which is 4% slip. At exactly 3000 rpm the relative speed would be zero, so the flux change and the torque would be zero; the 120 rpm of slip is what keeps the flux changing and the torque flowing.

questions.q: When a metal sheet moves through a magnetic field, the eddy current loop inside the field experiences a force. In what direction does this force act, and why?
options: The force is always opposite to the direction of motion of the sheet, because the eddy currents are an application of Lenz's law and oppose the change producing them, so they act as a brake
The force is in the same direction as the motion, so the sheet speeds up as it moves through the field
The force acts at right angles to the motion, making the metal sheet spin instead of slowing
There is no net force, because the eddy currents on either side of the loop exactly cancel
questions.explanation: Eddy currents are an application of Lenz's law: the magnetic fields they set up oppose the change in flux. The force on the eddy current loop is therefore always opposite to the direction of motion of the sheet, making it harder to move the metal — this retarding force is the basis of electromagnetic braking, and the lost kinetic energy is dissipated as heat.

questions.q: Outline the difference between a motor and a generator in terms of energy transformation. (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: A motor transforms electrical energy into rotational kinetic (mechanical) energy. A generator transforms mechanical (kinetic) energy into electrical energy. They are structurally the same device operated in opposite directions; the only difference being examined is the direction of the energy conversion.

criteria.descriptor: States a motor converts electrical energy into mechanical / rotational kinetic energy.
States a generator converts mechanical / kinetic energy into electrical energy.

questions.explanation: Name both forms of energy and the direction for each — don't just write 'energy is converted'. Electrical to mechanical is the motor; mechanical to electrical is the generator.
